name: Rickettsial Fever (Spotted Fever Group)

veryLikely: Rickettsia conorii / other spotted fever group Rickettsia species
possible: Orientia tsutsugamushi (if eschar is found on closer examination — would reclassify as scrub typhus)
pathogens.why: Spotted fever group rickettsioses are transmitted by ticks (rather than the chiggers/mites responsible for scrub typhus) and classically present with a generalized maculopapular or petechial rash rather than a single eschar, though clinical overlap exists and careful skin examination for an eschar should always be performed to distinguish from scrub typhus.

investigations.test: Careful skin examination for eschar and rash characterization
investigations.why: Helps distinguish spotted fever group rickettsiosis (maculopapular/petechial rash, no eschar) from scrub typhus (eschar), though management is similar.

investigations.test: Rickettsial serology (IgM/IgG, species-specific where available) or Weil-Felix (less specific)
investigations.why: Supports diagnosis, though treatment should not be delayed pending results when clinical suspicion is high.
Assesses organ involvement; thrombocytopenia and transaminitis are common supportive findings.

references: NCDC India Guidelines for Rickettsial Diseases
reasonSource: ()=>"Fever with maculopapular rash and headache, particularly with tick exposure history, is consistent with a spotted fever group rickettsial infection (distinct from scrub typhus, which classically presents with an eschar from chigger/mite bites rather than a generalized maculopapular rash from tick-borne transmission). Empiric doxycycline should be started promptly given the excellent and rapid response to treatment and the risk of progression if delayed."
